utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we return to the ambassador's evidence, can I just deal with two things? First can I request that we have half an hour this afternoon, perhaps at half past 3.00, to deal with the Rule 70 issue? The representatives concerned are available and the matter has got to be sorted out for the timetabling of the witness. That shouldn't interfere with cross-examination of this witness, either because by then there would have been enough time for cross-examination or because I understand the witness is prepared to stay on tomorrow if that's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let us deal with that first. What will be the application in relation to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It will be for the government concerned to come and make its position clear in a way that I simply can't make clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We had notification that there may be such an application, so we've had a chance to consider it, and we are not in favour of it. We don't think it appropriate. If counsel cannot make the matter plain, then we don't think it appropriate for governments to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I nevertheless have time at the end of the day to deal with it because I will be provided with more information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- and I will have the representative to assist me. And these are difficult matters, and indeed I've taken a course of dealing with them far more openly than they're typically dealt with. Because to date I think they've typically been dealt with in other Chambers on an entirely ex parte basis, and I've avoided doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Quite right, too, if I may say. Clearly, matters of this sort should, as far as possible, be dealt with openly. But you've heard our views.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. I'll convey those to the government concerned. But in any event, if we may provisionally have half past 3.00 as the time for dealing with that. Second, I want to be in a position to make a final decision about Vllasi, as well as to have a decision made about the other witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know you've had a summary. I've provided the fuller document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a statement. It's called investigator's notes, but it's effectively a draft summary. And it may be that we can have a few minutes in that half-hour session this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll read it during the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. And I believe you've already had a copy of the statement of the witness to whom the Rule 70 application relates so that you can consider him. And with that, we'll turn, if we may, to the evidence of the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Ambassador, I've been given an indication, really by sign language, I think, but I understand it to mean that can you and I leave a gap between question and answer, if we're not to incur the wrath of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We reached the stage yesterday where you were about, in your narrative, to leave Racak. You've given us your general conclusions, and you can be asked further questions about those. But one thing I hadn't asked you is this: One of the propositions that has been advanced since the discovery of the bodies at Racak was that the bodies had been in some way redressed, that their clothes had been taken off, and perhaps uniforms had been taken off, and they had been redressed as civilians. Of course, you're a layman, you don't have forensic scientific skills or medical skills, but nevertheless, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My firm layman's conclusion from what I saw on the ground, the positions of the bodies, the clothes worn, the bullet holes and the blood, the fact that it was in the middle of winter up a very slippery, steep slope, and any changing of clothes and that sort of thing would have to have been done in the darkness of night, in the middle of the night, and I consider that story, that version, that interpretation that somehow these bodies were redressed to be ludicrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've dealt in your statements in detail with what precisely happened as you returned from Racak, and I don't need to take you through that in any detail at all, but there is one proposition that's been raised and that has been the subject of evidence and that I'd like your help with and that's this: Telephone calls, if any, made either to OSCE officials, to NATO, or to United States officials between the time of your leaving Racak, or indeed while you were at Racak, and the time that you delivered the press statement in Pristina. What summary can you give us of your recollection of making phone calls and your explanation, if any, for what's been said about them?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been asked many times that question, and I sincerely have no recollection of myself talking to some of the people who have later said they talked to me. This would include people in Vienna with the OSCE and others. I have no doubt that I did tell others to make sure the news of what had happened that morning was conveyed to as many people as we could get it to. I certainly wanted OSCE headquarters, I wanted the capitals of the OSCE Member States to know what had happened. So I'm sure I told people to inform as many people as they wanted to. If people claim I spoke to them either while I was at Racak or on the way back or before the press conference, I have no doubt. I don't question that. I probably did. But there was so much happening at the time, I was so involved in the events that I saw on the ground, trying to figure out what it all meant and then, when I got back to the office, trying to construct what I was going to say at the press conference, I frankly have no memory, no recollection of -- of talking to any of these people. But this does not mean I did not. If they say I did, I'm quite sure they are not lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Back in Pristina, you eventually -- not eventually. You in due course made a press statement.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And first of all, give us of your account of that statement and then we'll look at the printed document itself.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I might have mentioned yesterday, when I was at Racak, a number of journalists asked me questions about what I had seen and what I thought of it, and I believe I made comments that I would try to recollect my thoughts and when I got back to Pristina, I promised to hold a press conference. When I got back to Pristina, I told my staff to put together a press conference, and that was done. Between my arrival and when the press conference started, I spent most of the time, if not all of it, in my office with my computer, trying to collect my thoughts and put it into a statement. The statement was essentially a description of what I had seen, a description of how the news came to the KVM the night before from General Loncar's office, and then my conclusions as to whether or not what we had been told by the government and what we had seen coincided, and my conclusion was they did not coincide. I said that on what I had seen -- again, I emphasise that I was not a specialist, I was not a crime scene investigator, but from what I had seen, the stories did not jibe. From what I have seen, it appeared to me to have been a number, perhaps as many as 40 or more, men and boys had been taken away, unarmed, and later turned up dead. I described it as a massacre. I said that I would hope that the government in Belgrade, if it disagreed with my conclusions, would admit trained criminal investigators so that they could go to the scene and determine what had in fact happened. I specifically mentioned investigators from this Tribunal. And I opened it up for questions. I think some of what I'm saying now, as my words that afternoon, came out in the questions and answers rather than in my formal introductory statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now look at the exhibit, please, which is in the bundle before the Judges at page 14, but here comes the exhibit itself to be separately produced. Sorry, not page 14, Your Honours. I gave you the wrong page. It's -- and it will become exhibit -- I think it's going to be Exhibit 229. No?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That should be the Exhibit 230.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 230. Thank you. And if the Chamber's happy to work with the exhibit just produced, this is the -- can we put a copy on the overhead projector, please, so that those viewing may see it? I'm sorry, I don't think it is in the bundle. It should have been. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Headed "Massacre of Civilians in Racak." It reads: "On the 15th of January, the KVM reported a serious deterioration of the situation in the Stimlje area. Racak, Malopoljce, Petrovo and Belince villages (south and west of Stimlje) were all affected. VJ and police forces prevented KVM patrols from entering the area but late in the afternoon the KVM patrol did get to the village of Racak. Verifiers saw one dead Albanian civilian and five injured civilians, including a woman and a boy, suffering from gunshot wounds. The KVM also received unconfirmed reports of other deaths in the area. Residents of Racak claimed that men had been segregated from women and children and that 20 males had been arrested and taken away. The verifiers took the details and evacuated the casualties before the onset of darkness." And had casualties been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next paragraph, in summary, asserts a wholesale violation of the cease-fire. The next paragraph speaks of verifiers - of teams, including verifiers, going to the village, and KDOM units sending patrols. The next paragraph sets out the accounts of surviving residents speaking of the killings taking place on the 15th of January and giving an account of the VJ and the police and security forces being involved. The next paragraph dealt with the arrival of the first KVM teams on the 16th of January and finding bodies in the houses and then the 23 male victims on high ground. The next paragraph touches on initial reports that led to your going to the village and your writing the following: "On arrival, villagers guided me to a site where I saw, much to my horror and shock, the bodies of over 20 men who had obviously been executed where they lay. I do not have the words to describe my personal revulsion, or that of all those who were with me, at the sight of what can only be described as an unspeakable atrocity. Although I only saw the bodies of 20, mostly elderly men, many shot at extremely close range, most shot in the front, back, and top of the head, KVM verifiers moved about and counted an additional number. "In all, 45 bodies were observed, including three women and one child. They were all in civilian clothes. All looked like humble village inhabitants. Although I am not a lawyer, from what I personally saw, I do not hesitate to describe the event as a massacre, a crime against humanity, nor do I hesitate to accuse the government security forces of responsibility. "The FRY government must produce the names of all involved in the police and VJ operations around Stimlje, who gave the orders, who executed those orders. The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia must come in, with visas, at the invitation of the FRY government, or without, to investigate this atrocity, and this must be accomplished in the next 24 hours." And the press release goes on to say further about the facts as verified by the KVM, and how that was violations of international humanitarian law, and how, in the last paragraph, you met with - or the last substantial paragraph - how you met with KLA representatives, who articulated their frustration and anger and indeed expressed their desire for revenge, although orders in the KLA headquarters were for continued restraint. Mentioning there of this Tribunal, what was the position of the then Prosecutor, Justice Louise Arbour, at about that time?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the following day I received a call from Judge Arbour, and we discussed what I had seen briefly and what I had said briefly, and I told her I thought it was very important that either she or people from this Tribunal, investigators, criminal investigators, come to Kosovo and do a thorough investigation. Judge Arbour reminded me that she had not been able to obtain a visa to enter the former Yugoslavia. She asked me if I thought it advisable for her to try to enter. I told her I thought that would be the best thing. I told her that if she was denied entry or her people were denied entry, that that would indicate that the government was not terribly serious about finding out what had happened at Racak. She said that she would personally get on a plane the following day, I believe it was, on the 18th, and try to enter via Skopje, Macedonia, in other words, the southern border. I told her I would send people down. I had something to do the following day. I can't remember what it was. I told her I would send some of my people down to try and facilitate her entry. I sent my French deputy, Mr. Keller. They went down, and I later received word that she had tried to make entry at the border, had been denied entry, and had been told she did not have the proper documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn from the press statement: The words used, did anybody else contribute to or cause you to use any of the words, or were they your choice?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My statement was totally my creation. These were all my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then can we move from the statement and the events at Racak to the fallout from it, which the Chamber can find at paragraph 64 and 65 of the second witness statement. What was the effect of your statement in Belgrade and indeed elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had immediate and, I would describe, dramatic impact. I had not anticipated as much impact as it seemed to have. But the following day we were receiving newspaper accounts and telephone calls from all over Europe, and elsewhere, talking about the events at Racak, asking about the events at Racak. There was a tremendous reaction to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The effect eventually on you was what, your status in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the reaction, I decided to drive to Belgrade and asked to see President Milosevic. Government representatives were already coming out with very critical comments on my statement, and I thought it best that I go and speak to Mr. Milosevic directly. My people asked for an appointment. We were told he's busy, so we sat in the hotel for I think most of the day, maybe longer. And at night, when I was going out to dinner, some journalists, some Serb journalists, came to the hotel and they asked me what I thought of having been declared persona non grata. And that was how I learned that the government had, in fact, issued a statement over the radio, over the media, without informing me that I had been given 48 hours to leave the country, that I was persona non grata.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In fact, were you forced out as quickly as that or were you able to stay with what was called frozen status or something?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE chairman in office went to President Milosevic. In various conversations, as I understand it, including a face-to-face discussion, at first my 48 hours was extended to, I think, 72 hours, and at the very last minute I was informed that an agreement had been reached that I was in something called a frozen persona non grata status, which I never quite heard defined and had never heard of before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the event, you didn't see the accused again?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You didn't see the accused again?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did, however, stay in Kosova until the withdrawal of the OSCE generally?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps in a sentence or so, just explain that withdrawal and your part in it.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Racak, the level of cooperation from government authorities, what little we had before Racak, disappeared. Our verifiers, our people, found themselves in increasingly difficult and dangerous situations when they were out and about patrolling. The chairman in office of the OSCE, after what he said were lengthy discussions with the principal players in the capitals of Europe and North America, called me and said, "Since you are finding it increasingly difficult to fulfil the mandate of the mission, and since things appear to be getting increasingly difficult in terms of security for your people," at first he asked me if I thought it would be wise to withdraw, and later he -- and I agreed that I thought it would be, and later he ordered me to withdraw the mission, in mid-March, late March.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as we've heard from other witnesses, everyone on the mission was got out, and I think that you stayed until the end and were the last person across the line, with General Drewienkiewicz.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is essentially correct. We thought we had gotten all 1.400 and some people out. A few days later, we discovered that two or three verifiers who had been on vacation or on leave and had not gotten the word that the mission had been withdrawn showed up in Belgrade. But essentially, we got everyone out under our evacuation plan, via Skopje; not only the people, but almost all of our equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I will ask you to look at a couple of other documents before we turn to a couple of events after your withdrawal. First of all, can we look at what's already been produced as Exhibit 94, tab 33, which is a statement I've just handed in. Then it can go straight on the overhead projector. 94, tab 33. This is a statement for the press issued by Milutinovic, the president. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember reading it, yes, when it came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can follow it on the screen to save time. "In the wake of the statement of Ambassador William Walker, head of the OSCE Verification Mission in Kosovo ... the President of the Republic ... made the following statement: "When yesterday ... police undertook to arrest terrorists who killed a police officer ... in a terrorist attack, in the vicinity of Racak...," and I'm skipping some words, "... terrorists attacked them from automatic weapons, portable launchers and mortars. The police had to respond to such terrorist savagery in line with their powers. The OSCE mission and Ambassador Walker were duly informed of undertaking the arrests. Immediately after the clash, an investigating team arrived at the scene headed by an investigating judge ... Danica Marinkovic and the Deputy District Prosecutor ... the terrorists, who took positions on the neighbouring hills, opened fire and prevented the investigation." Did you yourself see anything of Judge Marinkovic?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never met the lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you hear about her involvement at Racak?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I subsequently heard that she was the investigative judge in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on: "... on the 16th of January," in the statement, "the on-site investigation was once again prevented because William Walker demanded the investigating judge to go there without police protection, thereby preventing the competent judicial authorities from carrying out their legal obligations." Any truth in that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "However, at the same time, Ambassador Walker, accompanied by foreign and journalists of Albanian separatist newspapers whom he personally invited, visited the scene and took advantage of the absence of judicial and other state authorities so as to make the statement containing falsehoods and personal assessments which are totally baseless." Any truth in the particular assertions there about you inviting Albanian separatist newspaper journalists?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It goes on to make the following observations and I'll deal with them in a block to save time so far as we can. "He even went on so far as to personally assess what happened, to pass judgements and even to give orders what should be done next - and all that in a sovereign country. "In this act of deceiving the world opinion, according to well-known recipes attempting to stage some kind of new "Markale," Ambassador Walker secured the full protection of his proteges from the terrorist so-called "KLA." The series of lies and fabrications he accused our state authorities in an obvious attempt to divert the attention from terrorists, murderers and kidnappers and to once again protect them the way he had been protecting them all along. Ever since he came, he turned a blind eye only to the crimes of the terrorists. Security of citizens, security and responsibility of the police does not interest him, and in his today's statement he has passed judgements on the authorities of Serbia and Yugoslavia, their competent authorities, and accused them of "violating the cease-fire" - for what if not for protection of terrorists to whose crimes has remained silent." There's an assertion of bias and prejudice. What do you say to that, Ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say it's an incorrect interpretation of my actions and words. I tried to be as neutral and evenhanded as possible. I tried to denounce violence, kidnappings, assassinations wherever they occurred from what side they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just go to the end of last passages -- thank you very much. "The attacks on terrorists, even when launched from mortars and other heavy weapons he does not consider to be illegal. Such an attitude does not come for the first time to the fore in his statement and in his preventing that the investigating judge carry out her duty according to the oaths of her -- the laws of her own country. He probably forgot that he is not Governor or a Prosecutor or a Judge in Serbia or in the FRY but the representative of the organisation of 54 equal states and the head of the mission whose task is not to rule the country of a sovereign country but to observe and report accurately. By his statement of today, he forgot himself because he seems to favour the role of the prosecutor and the judge at the same time." Were you assuming such a role or were you, in your judgement, performing your duties as commissioned to do?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was charged with telling the OSCE what was happening in Kosovo, and what I was doing was trying to discharge that responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then, finally, I'll just deal with the first sentence of the next paragraph. "Even though it is indisputably clear that the police was provoked and compelled to defend itself from terrorist attacks, Mr. Walker ignored that fact and proclaimed the event as a conflict with the civilian population." Remind us again. Had the Serb forces taken any opportunity, in your visit to Racak, to explain the position or to get witnesses to talk to you, to explain the position? Or soldiers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. As I mentioned yesterday, we invited General Loncar to accompany us, and he declined. That was the only effort I saw to reach out and find out what the government was saying other than what we had heard from General Loncar the night before, the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And was there any evidence before you, suggested to be indisputably clear, that the police were provoked and compelled to defend themselves?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not before me, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there any evidence before you at any time of Serb casualties arising at Racak?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my statement, when the purported clash was described to us by General Loncar's office on the evening of the 15th, we had been told there were no government casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can take that document off the overhead projector and replace it with 94, Exhibit 94, tab 36, again to save time, and we'll see how your change of status was documented, or we'll look at part of this document. Starting at the top, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is a statement from the federal government and it's dated -- I haven't got the date. We'll see -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "At today's extraordinary session chaired by the Prime Minister Momir Bulatovic, the Federal Government considered the latest events in Kosovo and Metohija and the pressure put on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The government thinks it is a new campaign of the international community and decisively refused the groundless, false and malevolent assertions on events that took place in the village of Racak. "The federal government considered the activities of William Walker, Director of OSCE ... and concluded they are in flagrant --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, please slow down when reading. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "-- OSCE mission. Mr. Walker's activities went far beyond his mandate ...." Next paragraph. And move up one paragraph, please. It then says: "... Mr. Walker is to leave the Yugoslav territory within 48 hours," and then says this: "Regarding cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, the government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you are being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Regarding cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, the government confirmed Yugoslavia's readiness to fully implement the agreement signed with the Tribunal. However, The Hague Tribunal has no jurisdiction in Kosovo and Metohija whatsoever since the war is -- since the issue is not war but terrorism and our state's legitimacy to fight it. "The representatives of the Tribunal may come into our country -- in our country and negotiate on the realisation of the Agreement, but they can't inspect and investigate in Kosovo and Metohija." And you can read the rest. Just one thing, Ambassador, arising from that. It suggests here that there was no recognition of the right of this country to deal with terrorism. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion would be that a government certainly has a sovereign right to deal with terrorism but in a rational and reasonable fashion, not going in and essentially executing unarmed civilians in a village such as Racak, which is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. There are just two remaining topics, each of which I'll ask you to deal with succinctly but in your own manner, without my interruption, because I think it will be quicker. At Rambouillet, the Kosovo Albanian representatives did not sign. There was an adjournment, as it were. You took part or were present. Can you just explain why, in your judgement, they weren't prepared to sign at that first opportunity?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only attended the opening session of Rambouillet, having completed what was the KVM's mission, which was to get the Albanian delegation, including the KLA members, to Paris for the talks. I then returned to Pristina. At the conclusion of the first round of the Rambouillet talks, as you said, the Albanian delegation said it was ready to sign but was not going to sign and asked for a two-week break in the talks. When the Albanian delegation returned to Kosovo, I was asked to try to determine what had been on their minds, why they made this, "We are ready to sign but we're not going to sign at this moment. " So I went and talked to a number of the delegates who were in Rambouillet, and I talked to at least three KLA commanders and asked them to tell me why they had asked for the two-week delay. Their answer was something along the lines that while at Rambouillet, the delegation recognised that they were dealing with a historic moment for their people, for their constituents, and that what they signed their names to would be of incredible importance to their people. They also said that this was the first time in their memory that Albanians from Kosovo had been at a negotiating session in person, negotiating for their own future, and in their first encounter in international negotiations, they found they were dealing with Madeleine Albright, Robin Cook, the foreign ministers of Europe and North America, and they were somewhat overwhelmed with their own lack of experience in negotiations. They said that although they read the document they thought they could sign many times, they were worried, they were concerned that there might be some things in there that, with their inexperience, they were not totally grasping, and therefore they wanted to take some time out to go over this document. And they also wanted to touch base with their various constituencies to make sure that the Albanian population that they represented was truly in favour of their signing it. They told me that they had conducted whatever sort of survey they could do and had come to the conclusion that the Albanian population wanted peace, wanted their delegation to sign on their behalf. So they returned to Rambouillet, to France, and indicated their willingness now to sign.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second topic, different: The book or books "As Seen, As Told," prepared by the OSCE, just explain what triggered their preparation, bearing in mind that it may be the Chamber will be hearing in due course from Sandra Mitchell, who will be able to deal with methodology.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the mission terminated in Kosovo, we moved into Macedonia. Shortly after our exit, the NATO bombing campaign began, and also began an exodus from Kosovo of tens of thousands of refugees. This exodus overwhelmed the Macedonian government, the Albanian government. The people were put into very hastily constructed camps. Since I had 1.400 people who had recently been in Kosovo, who had worked with the Albanian population, we were asked by Mrs. Ogata from UNHCR, we were asked by the Macedonian authorities, by others, to help in the initial days of the camps. I visited, I think, most of the camps in Macedonia, and later visited some of them in Albania. The conditions were horrendous, and everywhere I went, people in the camps, not only in the camps - sometimes I visited villages where the people were living outside the camps, the refugees - people approached me and I heard story after story after story about what had happened in their villages while they were being driven out, et cetera. Sandra Mitchell was an officer on my staff in Kosovo who I had come to respect. I had given her the task of dealing with the human rights situation in Kosovo, and in our Macedonian exile, I asked her to put together a team to go to the camps and to collect as many of these stories of what had happened to these refugees. I told her that we wanted only first-person accounts. We didn't want hearsay; we didn't want people talking about things they had heard about, but only things that they had witnessed. Sandra put together a team of five or six people. I think some of them were lawyers. I remember specifically there was a Danish lady, a German lawyer, several other people from various nationalities. And they spent the remaining time that we were there as a mission in the camps compiling depositions, sworn depositions, as I say, of these tales of abuse, and that was eventually compiled into -- I'm sorry. I didn't know the title of the document, but what we call the OSCE Human Rights Report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. You will be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My further apologies for going too fast in the reading, to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Milosevic. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The microphone is on. The light is on. My question was: How long are you going to limit my cross-examination to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Three hours, no more. If you refrain from arguing with the witness, if you refrain from repeating the questions, if you ask short questions, you will be able for get much more done. So you follow that line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know that I've argued with witnesses. But let me say before I start that I expected that you would shorten the time for my cross-examination, in view of yesterday's proclamations with respect to Rule 92 bis, because Drewienkiewicz testified for two days, Maisonneuve also took two days, and their chief, according to you, should be exposed to cross-examination for three hours only, and I think that that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... further time, which is taken off your time for cross-examination. Now, move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well, Mr. May. I just said this for it to come out in the record, and not to waste time. The opposite side began its examination-in-chief yesterday with the diplomatic career of the witness, as a career diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that, by Clinton, in June 1993, you were nominated and appointed ambassador to Panama, and that it was on the basis of the position of the senate, and on that grounds, that he refrained from actually sending you there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My "nomination" is a bit overstating it. The Clinton White House was thinking about nominating me to go to Panama, but one senator objected. And in our system, one senator has the ability to impede a nomination and confirmation, so I did not go to Panama.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was the reason for this, for impeding this, as you termed it, amongst other things, your false testimony with respect to the deaths in Salvador, where you were ambassador?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The senator's reasons for opposing my nomination have never been made clear, either to me, nor to the State Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of "It's Official." That is the title of the Washington Post of the 16th of June, 1993, where it says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... officer William Walker, former ambassador to El Salvador and before that a diplomat in Bolivia, Honduras, Brazil and Peru, to replace Deane Hinton in Panama." [Interpretation] And then, two days later, also in the Washington Post, on the 18th of June, we have the following correction: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... on the nomination of career diplomat William Walker to be ambassador to Panama, as was reported here on Wednesday. There are hints of some Senate unhappiness with Walker, formerly ambassador to El Salvador..." [Interpretation] Did that have anything to do with the reactions of the Panama public and church?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea why the Washington Post said that, nor what the reaction of the Panamanian people and church might have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, then. Let me remind you of this, in connection with the fact that this challenging was linked to your previous work in El Salvador and the writings of the New York Times, for instance, on the 24th of April, 1990. Only the portions which make reference to you, so I'm not going to quote the entire newspaper article: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... Walker said there was no evidence the military was involved in the Jesuits' murder; rebels dressed in Government uniforms might have done it, he suggested. Those preposterous propositions were exploded five days later by President Cristiani's statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What's the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is -- may I just finish my quotation from this New York Times article, which I was quoting, because it talks about the Roman Catholic archbishop: [In English] "Four church women from the United States were murdered. Two US labour representatives were shot in the Sheraton Hotel as they met a land reform leader ... The murder of six Jesuit priests last November has brought the issue forward again. There is no doubt that the killers were in the armed forces; President Alfredo Cristiani said so on January 7... What is at stake is not just a minimum level of decency in El Salvador. It is our own honour."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true that you made a false representation of the events in El Salvador?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your Honour, might I explain the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was ambassador in El Salvador from 1988 until 1992. The murder of the nuns, the killing of the two labour leaders, both of whom were my friends, occurred well before I got there. During my period as ambassador, the guerrillas launched a final offensive in November of 1989, in which, as you say, and as the Washington Post and New York Times describe, six Jesuit priests were killed. When I made the statement that we did not know who had killed them, that men in uniforms with ski masks could have been either from the government military or from the guerrillas, this was before it was discovered who had actually done the killings. You say President Cristiani announced and took responsibility for his military in killing the Jesuits on the 6th or 7th of January. The embassy had already stated that on the -- I believe the 2nd of January. I have with me a letter, if you're interested, from the Congress of the United States, indicating what I did, what my embassy did, to investigate, determine who had killed the Jesuits, and then insist that those responsible - a colonel, several lieutenants, and soldiers - be brought to justice, and they were brought to justice and they were convicted. And as I say, it was with the full cooperation of Bill Walker, the ambassador, as well as his staff, as well as the US government, that that was the end of the Jesuit case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely where I wanted to continue. Again I'm going to quote the Washington Post on the 21st of March, 1993, the Sunday edition. It carried a long article: [In English] " ... Walker told a news conference after the murders. 'And it's not a management control problem that would lend itself to a Harvard Business School analysis.' On January 2nd, 1990, Walker told representative Joseph Moakley, Democrat Massachusetts in Washington that 'anyone can get uniforms... The fact that they [the killers] were dressed in military uniforms was not proof that they were military.' The same day that he met with Moakley, US Army Major Eric Buckland, a military advisor in San Salvador, told his superiors that a Salvadoran army officer had named Military Academy chief Colonel Guillermo Alfredo Benavides Moreno as the ringleader in the Jesuits' killing." [Interpretation] Therefore, this confirms that you gave an inaccurate statement, and later Cristiani dealt with it too. But what is of particular significance to me is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before we go any further, let's find out who wrote this article that you've been quoting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This article was carried by the Washington Post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've told us that. Who was it who wrote it so we may know who makes these allegations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hand it over to you as an exhibit. The length, 2.976 words. "Twelve Years of Torture..." is the headline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm asking for the reporter's name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [In English] Byline: Guy Gugliotta, Douglas Farah, Washington Post Foreign Service Body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Douglas Farah very well. He's a friend of mine, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Comment, if you can, on what is suggested here. It is said you made an inaccurate statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made an inaccurate statement, in hindsight. At the time I made it, it was what we knew, which was uniformed men had killed the priest. We did not know from whence they came; that on the 2nd of January I was in Washington speaking to Congressman Joe Moakley, also a friend, who was in charge of a committee of the Congress of the United States trying to get to the bottom of the Jesuit case. He asked me if we had uncovered the culprits. I told him we had not, that it could have been one side or the other. That same day, unbeknownst to me, in El Salvador, the case broke open when a major on my staff came forward and recounted a conversation he had with an El Salvadoran colonel, his counterpart, and it was revealed in that conversation that a unit of the Salvadoran army had killed the Jesuits. So what I am saying is that my statements throughout this were as accurate as I could make them at the time, but later, when it was discovered who had killed the Jesuits, as I say, I was then in the forefront of those trying to bring justice in the case, to bring military officers to justice, which was unprecedented in El Salvador. But the colonel, the two lieutenants, and some soldiers were in fact convicted after the United States government put incredible pressure on the Salvadoran government to bring these officers before a tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we've now spent the best part of quarter of an hour to 20 minutes on events in another continent a decade before. If it was an attempt to attack in some way the witness's credibility, you've had the opportunity of putting your case and the witness has dealt with it. Now, move on to some other topic more related to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, since you have limited my time, please allow me to use it the way I consider best. This is a witness who was obviously in charge of carrying out - how should I put this? - some sort of covert operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, when we come to that, you can put all that. But you're not wasting the time of the Court with events so long ago and of such little relevance. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 11th of December, 1989, St. Louis Post-Dispatch, in a long article -- I'm going to quote only a short excerpt: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... Jesuit colleges in the United States, accused the US Ambassador in El Salvador of trying to discredit the witness. In --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Your attempt to discredit this witness with events so long ago the Trial Chamber has ruled as irrelevant. Now, move on from El Salvador. You've been given your clear instructions. If you want to continue with the cross-examination, you must follow them, because the time of the Court is limited, and it cannot be taken up with irrelevant matters such as this. Now, move on to events closer to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is directly related to the continuity of the witness's activities. I'm going to move on from El Salvador. I'm just going to refer to yet another case which points to continuity in terms of such activities of the witness. It relates to Nicaragua. [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... filed in US district court by independent counsel Lawrence Walsh. Walker was responsible for setting up a phony humanitarian operation at an air base in Ilopango, El Salvador. That 'humanitarian' air base was used to run guns, ammunitions, and supplies to the fascist Contra mercenaries attacking the Nicaraguan Revolution. Walker was also the US ambassador to El Salvador from 1988 to -- from 1988 to 1992," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with the allegation. Mr. Walker, have you followed what the allegation is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, Your Honour. During my 40-year career as an American diplomat but especially during my -- the later years of my career as ambassador to El Salvador, as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Central America and Panama during the 1980s, you know, I, as well as the policy -- policies that I was implementing, have come in for a great amount of criticism in the free press of the United States and the press of the world, as a matter of fact. It is not surprising to me that you can bring articles up that make allegations like that. All I can say is this is, you know, water off my back, press criticism of US policies and the person who was implementing them, Bill Walker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The allegation appears to be that in Nicaragua or in El Salvador, it's not clear, a humanitarian base was used to run guns, ammunition, and supplies, et cetera. Is it a matter on which you could comment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. The -- as Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Central America during the late 1980s, this was later condensed into the word "Contragate," I was responsible for bringing humanitarian assistance to the Contras, which was a policy that had been confirmed by the US Congress several times. Unbeknownst to me, unbeknownst to the State Department, unbeknownst essentially to the world, a colonel, Oliver North, in the National Security Council was doing things that were eventually determined by Judge Walsh and his commission to be illegal, and that had to do with the supply of armaments to the Contras. The base, the air base that was mentioned, Ilopango, is in El Salvador. That is where we were bringing in humanitarian supplies, as I said, that I was responsible for, and sending them on to the Contras. Oliver North and some other people were using that same air base to bring in illegal supplies, i.e., armaments. The Walsh report noted this, that the same air base had been used for both types of supplies, legal and illegal. The Walsh report, as I said, did not in any way imply that the supply of humanitarian material to the Contras was either illegal or, you know, should not have taken place. That was, as I said, a policy that had been approved by the Congress several times. Does that explain it, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the policy was humanitarian assistance. Please comment on this: It relates to you. [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... "in Kosovo. This time his actions give backing to different Contra army, the Contra Kosovo Liberation Army." [Interpretation] Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who again? What are you quoting from, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I put a question. So I'll tell you what I've quoted. Never mind. That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right or is that not right? The question is -- I'm quoting myself. Let's put it that way. Is that right or is that not right? I'm quoting Gary Wilson. I'm quoting an article by Gary Wilson. Is this right or is this not right?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question. If the question is was either I or were the people of the KVM supplying the KLA, the Albanian population, with assistance during my tenure as head of the KVM, the answer is no, we were not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was that the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question was: Did you -- you were giving your backing to a different Contra army, the KLA. I think you've answered the point. Would you -- I suppose, put it this way: Did you back the KLA during your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we did not. We often condemned the KLA for acts of violence. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get precisely to that. And now in relation to this, this linkage in respect of such activities, in relation to Racak, it says: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... the site of the alleged massacre and declared that he knew all the facts. He was the judge, jury, and executioner all in one. Not even a district attorney in any United States city could so boldly make such a declaration: Guilty first, evidence later." And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with that allegation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I'm not sure what the quotation is from or what I'm dealing with. If the question is did I consider myself judge, jury, and executioner all in one, my answer is no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, Mr. Walker, since it is claimed: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... Walker? Is he the Richard Butler of Kosovo, as many in the Balkans now believe?" [No translation] [In English]... "[Previous translation continues]... Kosovo team was a spy team like the UNSCOM group in Iraq, Walker replied, `I hope everyone on my mission is trying to gather as much intelligence as they possibly can.' Questioned again, 'Are you reporting it back to Washington?' Walker reported -- Walker replied, 'A lot of it comes back to Washington, but it goes to all capitals" and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us hear -- let us hear where this quotation is from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a quotation from Gary Wilson's article too. But I assume that he is not challenging --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When and where did Gary Wilson write this article?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I haven't got that here now, but you can take it from a website that I'm going to give you. This is the website: [In English] US-Kosovo Policy -- [Interpretation] Here's the website so you can check it exactly, the date and everything else. Unfortunately, I do not have everything I need here so that I could know all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, were you really involved in these activities, Mr. Walker? Was this the main thrust of your activities, parallel to the official mission that you were conducting?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was pursuing my official mission, which was to try to tell the OSCE and the capitals of the member states of the OSCE as much as we could possibly gather in terms of the reality of what was happening in Kosovo. That was our job. We were verifiers, which implies gathering information and telling people about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Only that?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As the mission progressed from the beginning, we took on other tasks, a number of which were at your direction. You might recall when you told me that two journalists had been kidnapped by, as you call them, the so-called KLA, and you told me that you expected my mission to get them released. So that started a process in which we tried to do that several times, including the release later of some VJ soldiers who were captured by the KLA as well as some people from the KLA that your forces had taken prisoner. So we -- we got involved in that sort of activity. I was also asked by the Serb community in Kosovo to try and determine what had happened to members of their families who had disappeared. So what I am saying is that, over time, the mission took on other tasks besides the collection of information and the dissemination of that information to the OSCE and beyond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I put a question not only in relation to the information that you have been speaking about but also in relation to intelligence information. I'm going to quote the Sunday Times for you, London, the 12th of March, 2000: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... "Kosovo guerrilla army. American intelligence agents have admitted they helped to train the Kosovo Liberation Army before NATO's bombing of Yugoslavia. ... Central Intelligence Agency officers were cease-fire monitors in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999, developing ties with the KLA and giving American military training manuals and field advice," et cetera, et cetera. "Many of its satellite telephones and global positioning systems were secretly handed to KLA... Several KLA leaders had the mobile phone number of General Wesley Clark, the NATO Commander. ... The American agenda consisted of their --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness deal with these allegations, series of allegations here being made and quoted by you. The first suggestion is that, Ambassador -- Let the witness deal with these allegations. What's suggested is there were cease-fire monitors who were CIA officers developing ties with the KLA and giving American military training, et cetera. First of all, is there any truth in that suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there is, it's not to my knowledge. I knew of no personnel on KVM staff who were either with the CIA nor who were giving training to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And it's said that many telephone and global positioning systems were handed to the KLA and the leaders had the telephone number of General Clark. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not. I know that the KLA did do most of its communications via cell phones and that sort of thing. Where they got them, how they acquired them, who they communicated with, I have no personal knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that same article, precisely in relation to what you have been saying now, that you know nothing about this, it says -- this is the Sunday Times that I have been quoting: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... dismissed suggestions that he had wanted war in Kosovo, but admitted the CIA was almost certainly involved in the countdown to airstrikes." So that's inaccurate. Is that right, Mr. Walker?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I -- let me reread your quote here. I do dismiss --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While he's doing it, might we know the author of this document and if this is allegation against the witness directly but the text --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. Sunday Times, 12th of March, 2000, Tom Walker, [In English] Aidan Laverty. A-i-d-a-n, Aidan Laverty. Tom Walker and Aidan Laverty, from Sunday Times, London, 12th of March, 2000. "CIA aided Kosovo guerrilla army." [Interpretation] All right. Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Let the witness just deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do dismiss suggestions that I wanted war in Kosovo. I have probably said numerous times that I'm sure the CIA was interested in what was happening in Kosovo, as I'm sure the intelligence services of a number of countries, including your own, were interested in what was happening in Kosovo. I am not with the CIA. I have never been with the CIA. I have worked with members of the CIA, but as I said, not in connection with Kosovo. So I -- as I say, I'm sure the CIA was interested in knowing what was going on. I'm sure they read our reports, OSCE reports. What Tom Walker of the London Times derived from this, I know not. THE ACCUSED [Interpretation] All right. Before I move on to my next question, I would like to -- I've been trying to communicate with that lady by sign language but apparently she can't see me. I have a video cassette here, and I would like to have it played, please. The footage is very short. Very short video clips. And I kindly ask the technical service to play the video clips one by one and that is what I shall request. I don't know whether the technical people can actually hear me as I say this. So it's a series of different video clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While they arrange this, Mr. Walker, do you know a Canadian officer, historian, Roly Keith? He has several diplomas. He has served with the Canadian military for 30 years, also with NATO, an historian. He was head of your office in Kosovo Polje, of the Verification Mission in Kosovo Polje. Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that name whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You'll probably remember him. Mr. Walker, in your statement, you say on page -- well, let me not quote it now. I'll quote it if you think it's not that way. You talk about the NATO aggression. Is it correct that NATO bombed Yugoslavia because America and its Secretary of State, Madeleine Albright, wanted war?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my understanding of why NATO began the bombing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please, could you play the first video clip. I hope that you will recognise -- well, could we also have the sound track, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] America, headed by Madeleine Albright, Secretary of State, judging by various sources like Time Magazine, wanted war, and Yugoslavia was a sacrificed lamb or a target. And this was a way of rallying Europe together in the twenty-first century. It is clear that President Milosevic - I have no intention of defending him or attacking him - was elected president three times. Yugoslavia has been a democratic country for quite some time now, and it's quite irrelevant whether you like him or not. And that cannot be a justification or an excuse."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a member of the Verification Mission, head of the office of the Verification Mission in Kosovo Polje, an officer of the Canadian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will ask the witness whether he recognises the gentleman or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman's views are quite irrelevant. If you want to call him as a witness, you can, but you're not going to examine this witness about him. It's merely his views. Now, do you want to play any more of your tape?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. You'll see more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll do it after the adjournment. And you're not to ask any questions about that. That was merely the views of that man, and he can give evidence in due course if he wants. Mr. Walker, could you be back, please, in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I don't understand how you can limit my right to ask the witness to comment on the statements made by an officer who was a member of his mission and upon whose findings his report was in fact based. I don't understand that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He does not know the man who was on the television. The comments relate to the very issues which we're going to have to decide, and it's not a matter for the man on the television or for this witness; it's a matter for this Trial Chamber, which is going to have to decide these issues. Yes. Now, continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. I shall endeavour to get an answer. But does that mean that we have noted that Mr. Walker claims that this particular officer was not a member of the mission and was not an authentic person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He said -- what the witness said was that he didn't recognise the man.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What does that mean, that he didn't recognise him? It means that he cannot comment on his positions, if it is an officer who was head of a department in the mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that during your stay at the head of the KVM, the police was a professional police force and that cooperation with the police force was good?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the Serb police, there was a certain amount of cooperation; however, there were a number of incidents, including one that I was personally involved in, where I would have to say it was as unprofessional, as uncooperative as anything I've seen in my career with a purportedly professional police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, your member - precisely, the one that they won't let me quote here - says that they got on very well and that they performed their duties professionally, and he was in the field, and not you. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Mr. Milosevic, I do not recognise the person that was on the screen. We had over 1.400 members of the mission. I certainly knew only a small portion of that. I did not know this gentleman. He might have had very good relations with the police. As I said, I had at least one incident involving me personally in which a policeman came at me with a hand grenade, and I would hardly consider that to be professional police behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Walker, in your statement, you devote two whole pages to the fact that a drunken policeman had an argument with the members of your security detail and that he apologised to you, in fact, and that you never saw the hand grenade yourself. And I don't see that this incident deserves this kind of attention that you are attributing to it. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally thought it was a very serious incident. My security and the security of a number of people from the mission were involved. As you say, he was drunk, he was armed, and members of my security detail saw the grenade and whisked me away from his presence. When I returned, in very broken and drunken English, I believe he was trying to apologise. I thought the incident was serious enough to ask for an investigation by General Loncar. He promised to do so. He came back within a few hours and told me essentially that we had imagined the whole thing, that it was the fault of my unarmed security detail and that they had provoked this drunken, armed, grenade-carrying policeman; in other words, just the exact opposite of what had occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Not to dwell on that point, you yourself said that it was established that he wasn't on duty and no weapons were used, as it says in your statement. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Loncar told me that he was an off-duty policeman from Belgrade. He said that the man was not drunk. He said the man was not armed. I personally saw a Kalashnikov rifle in his car, which the police put in the police car when they took him away, wearing a ski mask, shortly after the incident had occurred. I thought that was also fairly unprofessional police behaviour, to put a man who was supposedly in detention in the back seat of a police car, with a weapon at his side, and allowing him to go away with a mask over his face. But I am not a professional policeman myself. Maybe this is professional behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not waste time, because I have many more important topics to cover. You talk about ethnic cleansing in your statement. Do you know -- or rather, could you comment on, for example, a statement made by the member of your mission, who says: "I can testify to the fact that in February and March 1999 there was no genocide. When it comes to ethnic cleansing, I was not present nor did I see events which could be characterised as ethnic cleansing. In connection to my previous answer, I wish to state that I was witness to a series of incidents, and most of them were caused by the KLA, for which the security forces, aided by the army, reacted." Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before the witness answers, we need to know who has made this statement and when he made it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This same officer made this statement, and I have this on the tape too, which you won't allow me to play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. The officer, whose name was given, the Canadian, apparently said at some stage that he didn't see any ethnic cleansing. You can see, Mr. Walker, on the screen what it is alleged. Perhaps you can then comment on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't comment on what he saw or didn't see. Any comments I've made about evidence of ethnic cleansing was based on my own observations and those of other members of my staff. Who this gentleman was and why he made those statements, I have absolutely no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You speak about refugees. Could you comment on the following statement, made by this officer of yours: "In the past weeks or ten days in Kosovo, we continued receiving reports on hundreds and sometimes thousands of refugees from our area of responsibility. However, when my observers and I went to these locations, we would come across just several tens of refugees. This does not mean that there were not a hundred people on the move, but they were taken in very quickly by their relatives from Pristina or they took to the hills or somewhere else. And it was not ethnic cleansing - at least, that is not what I imply by that term - and even less was it a genocide. I was not witness to mass human rights violations. What I did see, and the things I did attend, were events which turned into a civil war very quickly, a burgeoning one, between the rebels, terrorists, as they were called by the security forces, and the security forces themselves, who were trying to protect and defend the communication devices throughout Kosovo." Was that so or not? Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I again have no idea what this man was referring to, whether he's referring to refugees before the bombing, during the bombing. I certainly saw tens of thousands of refugees in the refugee camps that I referred to earlier, in Macedonia and Albania. They were all Albanians. Again, this gentleman, I have no idea where he was, what he was doing, who he was talking to, so I can hardly comment on his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I informed you a moment ago that he was the head of your office, the head of your bureau in Kosovo Polje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has responded that he cannot comment on what the man claims to have seen. As I've said, if you want to call him as a witness, it's open to you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question wasn't whether he knew him. He said he didn't know him, but I asked him to comment what the man had stated. But we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the army and MUP recognised the agreement and abided by the agreement and that the KLA did not, the one that was achieved between Holbrooke and myself?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, in our meeting in November, I reported to you that there was non-compliance on both sides; i.e., the MUP, the VJ, and the KLA were all doing things that were specifically prohibited by the agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can you comment on this: It is the statement where the officer claims that he was in villages in Kosovo, and, as you know, the KLA controlled for one year 50 per cent of the territory, a year before that. The security forces did not enter those areas, in keeping with the Holbrooke-Milosevic agreement, but the KLA did not stop at its own territory. They would keep effective skirmishes and moving into that territory, and so on and so forth. Now, asked whether they supported the KLA, the answers were unclear, when the population was asked, in fact. Can I have your comments to that, please.

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not again entirely sure what the question is, Mr. Milosevic. I will repeat: The KVM, neither I nor any person on the mission who was doing what they were supposed to be doing, was in any way helping one side or the other. We were there to determine what the sides were doing and whether or not they were in compliance with the agreements that your government signed. I would have to comment on your bringing up the question of whether or not the KLA controlled territory. I specifically remember you telling me when I asked you about what we thought was our need to bring in a helicopter ambulance capability, with a Swiss helicopter, and I explained that we would need this if any of our people were injured, either deliberately or accidentally, while in territory controlled by the KLA, and you were offering a government helicopter to do that extraction, and you told me quite categorically that the KLA controlled no territory in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The point was that the KLA was attacking, and not that it was controlling the territory. He mentioned one year previously, that they were in control one year previously, but it was the attacking that I was asking about. But let's move on. Your cooperation, did it have to do with helping separatism? Is that true? How can you comment, for example, on this assertion: "On the basis of everything we know, I think that we in fact assisted the separatist movement and that the idea of a multicultural Kosovo was disappearing, just like the Serbs, the Romas, and Jews which were killed and forced to flee to save their own skins." Is that observation correct or not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The observation that the KVM somehow was trying to promote separatism is ludicrous. It is not true. If there were individuals, again, who felt one way or the other about separatism, that I cannot comment on, but the mission, as I was instructed, had nothing to do with encouraging, promoting, advocating separatism.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you claim that all the people you talked to said that they had fled from Kosovo because of the threats that were being made to them by the police and not NATO. Could you comment on that statement made by your officer? And it was the following: "A justification for war which can also be brought into question was the alleged ethnic cleansing and jeopardising of human rights which were allegedly committed when my colleagues and I were in Kosovo. This did not happen. The refugees were not fleeing Kosovo in the spring, while we were there, up until the time that NATO started the war on the 24th of March. According to my information, the UN Refugee Committee informed us that the first wave of refugees crossed the border only on the 27th of March, in large numbers. As you mentioned, hundreds of thousands of refugees and displaced persons are the results of the civil war, but first and foremost are the results of the NATO bombing." That is what your officer claims. Is that true or is it not?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Milosevic, you are asking me to comment on statements made by a member of the KVM, for whatever reason he made those, and on the basis of what evidence he made those, I have no information. If you're asking me, you know, what provoked the exodus of refugees, massive exodus of refugees during the NATO bombing campaign, I spoke to hundreds and hundreds of refugees in the camps. I did not find a single one who said they had fled the bombing; on the contrary, some of them said they wished there had been more bombing. They all said they had fled the horrors, the mistreatment, the killings they saw, at the hands of your security forces. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's quite clear to me. But this man is not speaking on the basis of I don't know what facts which he read somewhere, but on the basis of his immediate involvement and work in Kosovo and Metohija, and that's why I asked for your comments. My next question is the following: Is it correct that the KLA was the armed road to realising the idea of a Greater Albania?

utterances.speaker: WILLIAM WALKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no basis for answering that question. I do not know what the agenda of the KLA was at any point during the conflict, other than to protect the Albanian population, that they thought were their constituents, from harm.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to ask that we take a look at Exhibit 11 from this tape. It is not the officer, Mr. May; it is a clip from Albanian television. And I'd like to ask the technical booth to pinpoint that particular section. It is number 11. You have got one over. You have 9, and then we come to 11, and it is a speech by KLA officers talking about what I have just been referring to. So it is number 11 on the tape.
